question: A manager spends the week in meetings, approving plans and training two hires. What did Intel’s Andy Grove say was her output?
options: The decisions and plans she made
What the teams she influences produce
How well she did her own tasks
answer: What the teams she influences produce: her own group’s output plus that of neighbouring groups she sways. When Grove asked middle managers, they listed judgements, plans and people trained; he called those activities, not output. So her hour counts by what it changes, like a short, well-aimed talk that shapes weeks of someone’s work.
move: Judge your work by what changes around you, not by how busy you were.
trap: ‘The decisions and plans she made’: activity feels like output.
simply: A football coach never scores a goal. You can still tell a good coach: the team plays better. Managers are the same: you judge them by how their team does, not by how busy they look.
why: Busy days feel productive, yet a day of meetings and emails can change nothing. Asking what your work changed for the people around you, a teammate unblocked, a mistake caught early, shows which hours mattered.

book.title: High Output Management
book.author: Andrew S. Grove
book.badge: By the Intel CEO named Time’s Man of the Year in 1997

source: Andrew S. Grove, High Output Management, 1983
reference: Andrew S. Grove, High Output Management (Random House, 1983; Vintage, 1995), ch. 3, Managerial Leverage
